source.title: Trimer covers in the triangular grid: twenty mostly open problems

accepted.question_text: Let the (a,b)-benzel be the finite region of unit hexagonal cells in the triangular lattice whose cell centers (i,j,k) satisfy i+j+k=1 and −(a−1) ≤ j−i, k−j, i−k ≤ b−1. Let T_ijk(a,b) denote the number of tilings of this region when right-pointing stones are allowed iff i=1, left-pointing stones are allowed iff j=1, and exactly k of the three bone orientations are allowed. Find an exact formula for T_003(k(3k−1)/2, k(3k+1)/2).

evidence.quote: Then the (a, b)-benzel consists of those cells whose centers (i, j, k) satisfy −(a−1) ≤ j−i, k−j, i−k ≤ b−1.

For 0 ≤ i, j ≤ 1 and 0 ≤ k ≤ 3 we define Tijk(a, b) as the number of ways to tile the (a, b)-benzel if the set of allowed prototiles contains the right stone iff i = 1, contains the left stone iff j = 1, and contains k of the bones.
Problem 1: Find an exact formula for T003(k(3k − 1)/2, k(3k + 1)/2).

Let T_012(a,b) count tilings of this region by left-pointing stones together with exactly two of the three bone orientations. Is it true that T_012(3n, 3n) = 2^n n! for every n ≥ 1?

Problem 2: Is it true that T012(3n, 3n) = 2^n n! for n ≥ 1?
Comment: Colin Defant, Rupert Li, Benjamin Young and I worked on problem 2 during the conference and later succeeded in solving Problems 2 and 3; see [3].

accepted.question_text: Let the (a,b)-benzel be the finite region of unit hexagonal cells in the triangular lattice whose cell centers (i,j,k) satisfy i+j+k=1 and −(a−1) ≤ j−i, k−j, i−k ≤ b−1. For any simply connected region tileable by stones and bones, the Conway-Lagarias invariant is the total area of the right stones minus the total area of the left stones, and it depends only on the region. Is it true that whenever the Conway-Lagarias invariant of the (a,b)-benzel is nonpositive, there exists a tiling of type 013, meaning a tiling using left-pointing stones and all three bone orientations but no right-pointing stones?

evidence.quote: Then the (a, b)-benzel consists of those cells whose centers (i, j, k) satisfy −(a−1) ≤ j−i, k−j, i−k ≤ b−1.

for any simply-connected region in the hexagonal grid that can be tiled by stones and bones, the total area of the right stones minus the total area of the left stones does not depend on the specific tiling but only depends on the region being tiled. This is the Conway-Lagarias invariant of the region.
Problem 4: Is it true that when the Conway-Lagarias invariant associated with the (a, b)-benzel is negative or zero, tilings of type 013 exist?

accepted.question_text: Let the (a,b)-benzel be the finite region of unit hexagonal cells in the triangular lattice whose cell centers (i,j,k) satisfy i+j+k=1 and −(a−1) ≤ j−i, k−j, i−k ≤ b−1. Let T_102(a,b) count tilings of this region by right-pointing stones together with exactly two of the three bone orientations. Is it true that for k ≥ 0 and n ≥ 1, except (k,n)=(0,1), one has T_102(n+3k, 2n+3k−1) = ∏_{i=1}^k ((2i)! (2i+2n−2)!)/((i+n−1)! (i+n+k−1)!)?

Problem 5: Is it true that T102(n + 3k, 2n + 3k − 1) = ∏_{i=1}^{k} ((2i)!(2i + 2n − 2)!)/((i + n − 1)!(i + n + k − 1)!) for k ≥ 0 and n ≥ 1 (except (k, n) = (0, 1))? Equality has been verified for 0 ≤ k ≤ 5, 1 ≤ n ≤ 5.

accepted.question_text: Consider tilings of a finite simply connected region in the hexagonal grid by stones and bones. A 2-flip is either the local move that replaces two oppositely oriented stones by two bones, or the local move that replaces a stone and a bone by a stone of the same orientation together with a bone of a different orientation. Can every such tiling be transformed into every other such tiling by a sequence of 2-flips?

evidence.quote: There are two natural kinds of ‘2-flips’ that can turn one stones-and-bones tiling into another; the first trades two stones of opposite orientation for two bones, and the second trades a stone and a bone for a stone of the same orientation and a bone of a different orientation.
Problem 19: Can every tiling of a finite simply-connected region using stones and bones be mutated into every other such tiling by means of a succession of 2-flips?

accepted.question_text: Let T_n be the triangular region of hexagonal cells with n cells on each side. Restrict to values of n congruent to 0, 2, 9, or 11 modulo 12, since exactly for those n the region can be tiled by stones alone. As n tends to infinity through that set, does the number of stone tilings of T_n converge 2-adically to 0?

evidence.quote: Those three authors showed that if one uses stones alone, Tn can be tiled by T2’s precisely when n is congruent to 0, 2, 9, or 11 (mod 12).
Problem 20: As n goes to infinity within the set of natural numbers congruent to 0, 2, 9, or 11 (mod 12), does the number of tiling of Tn by stones converge 2-adically to 0?
